hook.line: Hernando's memoir is full of things that happened after a long fight with himself: the job he swore he would never take, the secret he finally told. Spanish has a neat way to say "in the end, I did it anyway".
hook.es: Al final acabé por vender el taxi.
hook.en: In the end I ended up selling the taxi.

examples.en: We ended up laughing about it.

examples.es: Si sigues así, acabarás por enfermarte.
examples.en: If you carry on like this, you'll end up getting sick.
Did you end up talking to her? (to a friend)

examples.es: Tomás no terminó por vender el café.
examples.en: Tomás didn't end up selling the café.
We ended up eating at home.

rule:
To say you ended up doing something, usually after some resistance or a long road, use *acabar por* or *terminar por* plus the infinitive: *acabó por confesarlo*. You can also drop the *por* and use the gerund: *acabamos riéndonos*. Both mean the same.

The verb carries the tense: *acabé*, *acabarás*, *terminaron*. What follows stays in the infinitive or gerund.

Watch out: *acabar de* is a different thing. *Acaba de llegar* means "he has just arrived". And if nothing was in the way, you just use the plain verb.
smallPrint: Teachers call this a resultative periphrasis: a verb that frames the outcome at the end of a process.

options: He ended up accepting the offer.
He has just accepted the offer.
He refused the offer.
He ended up accepting the offer.
He will accept the offer.
He has just accepted the offer.
We stopped laughing about it.
We ended up laughing about it.
We were laughing at the end of the matter.
I had just understood it.
I never ended up understanding it.
I did not want to understand it.
They refused to sell the premises.
They finished cleaning the premises.
They ended up selling the premises.
Will you end up forgiving him?
Did you forgive him?
Are you forgiving him right now?
They stopped fighting.
They were fighting at the end.
They ended up fighting.
I just believed him.
I ended up believing him.
I will believe him.

yourTurn.prompt: Choose *acabó por* or *acabó de*: "He ended up telling everything."
yourTurn.why: *Acabar por* is "ended up"; *acabar de* would mean "has just".

yourTurn.prompt: Ask a friend: "Did you end up buying the car?"
yourTurn.why: The verb takes the *tú* ending and the action follows in the infinitive.

yourTurn.prompt: Say: "We ended up laughing about it."
yourTurn.why: With the gerund there is no *por*; with *por* you need the infinitive.

yourTurn.prompt: Make it negative: *Tomás acabó por vender el café.*
yourTurn.answer: Tomás no acabó por vender el café.
accept: Tomás no terminó por vender el café.
Tomás no acabó vendiendo el café.
Tomás no terminó vendiendo el café.
yourTurn.why: *No* goes right before the conjugated verb.
Only *acabar* changes for the future; *perdonarlo* stays as it is.

yourTurn.prompt: Say with a gerund and no *por*: "They ended up fighting."
yourTurn.why: A gerund after *acabar* or *terminar* works on its own, with no *por*.

yourTurn.prompt: Ask a stranger politely (*usted*): "Did you end up speaking to the owner?"

pitfalls.wrong: Acabó de aceptar la oferta. (meaning: he ended up accepting)
pitfalls.why: *Acabar de* means "has just"; for "ended up" use *por* or a gerund.
Use *por* with an infinitive, or no *por* with a gerund, never both.

pitfalls.wrong: Acabé por llegar a las ocho.
pitfalls.right: Al final llegué a las ocho.
pitfalls.why: *Acabar por* hints at a struggle or a long wait; for a plain event use the plain verb.

personal: Think of something you swore you would never do, and did anyway. Say it with *acabar por* or *terminar*: *Acabé por…*
